# Worked example: southern hake

This chapter fits the sex-structured model to a real, strongly dimorphic stock: southern hake
(*Merluccius merluccius*, ICES hke.27.8c9a). Females grow much larger than males (Linf 110 vs
74 cm), so the catch of large fish is almost all female. The inputs come from the Stock
Synthesis (SS3) assessment, which also gives a benchmark. The chapter

1. estimates dome-shaped selectivity for all fleets;
2. compares the sex-structured model with a sex-aggregated model that ignores the sex structure,
   including the residuals;
3. estimates life-history parameters of both sexes with penalties;
4. shows what these fits tell the SS3 assessment.

## Data from the SS3 assessment

`data(hake)` holds the inputs built from the SS3 output with r4ss and ss3diags2
(`inst/extdata/make_hake.R`):

```{r hk-data}
data(hake)
names(lfd_hake)
ss3_hake$mirror
ss3_hake$sex_minlen
```

* **Fisheries:** trawlers (retained and discarded fish), volpal (longline), artisanal and
  cdTrw (a small trawl fleet). SS3 has quarterly length compositions; they are raised to annual
  catch at length with the SS3 catch numbers by season and partition, as FLicc expects for
  samples spread over the year.
* **Surveys:** SpSurv and PtSurv are sexed; CdSurv is unsexed.
* **CPUE fleets:** the two indices of the assessment mirror the selectivity of trawlers and volpal
  and have no length data, so their selectivity is that of these fisheries; they are not separate
  FLicc gears (and would enter the planned FLicc-SPM model through these gears).
* **Small fish not sexed:** in the sexed surveys the fish below 21 cm are not sexed. SS3 combines
  the sexes in those bins and stores them as females. `settings$sex_minlen` treats them the same
  way (chapter *Sex structure*); without it, the small fish would be read as a large excess of
  females.

```{r hk-lfd, fig.height = 5}
plot_lfd(FLQuants(lapply(lfd_hake[c("trawlers", "volpal", "artisanal", "PtSurv")],
                         function(q) q[, ac(2022:2024)])),
         type = "prop", sex_minlen = ss3_hake$sex_minlen)
```

## Life history by sex

The growth, maturity, weight and natural mortality are those of the SS3 assessment. Male growth
and M are set in SS3 as offsets from the females (male Linf = 110 × e^−0.4^ = 73.7 cm). M declines
with age in SS3; here it is M at length, `m_model = "inverse"`, $M(L) = M\,L_{ref}/L$ with
$L_{ref}$ = female L50, which follows the SS3 values within about 0.03 over the sizes caught.

```{r hk-lh}
lhpar_hake
stk_hake <- stocklen_sex(lfd_hake, lhpar_hake, m_model = "inverse")
```

```{r hk-lh-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_growth(stk_hake, sex = "F") + ggplot2::ggtitle("Females")
plot_growth(stk_hake, sex = "M") + ggplot2::ggtitle("Males")
plot_m(stk_hake)
```

## Set-up

* The cdTrw fleet takes about 4% of the catch; its catch is added to the trawlers and its length
  data are not used.
* PtSurv is the survey: it is sexed, covers 15-50 cm and fits well. SpSurv mostly samples fish
  below 21 cm whose numbers vary with recruitment, and CdSurv is unsexed; both add little and are
  left out here.
* The fit uses the most recent years, 2017-2024: a short window suits the equilibrium assumption
  (similar conditions in all years) and constant selectivity. With 2010-2024 the domes make the
  early years more optimistic than SS3.
* Female Linf has a weak penalty (log-scale SD 0.1) around the 110 cm of the assessment.

```{r hk-setup}
yy <- ac(2017:2024)
gears <- c("trawlers", "volpal", "artisanal", "PtSurv")
lfd <- FLQuants(lapply(lfd_hake[gears], function(q) q[, yy]))
cbg <- FLQuants(lapply(catch_hake, function(q) q[, yy]))
cbg$trawlers <- cbg$trawlers + cbg$cdTrw
cbg <- FLQuants(cbg[c("trawlers", "volpal", "artisanal")])
set <- list(obs_model = "mn", surveys = "PtSurv", sex_minlen = ss3_hake$sex_minlen["PtSurv"])
ss3 <- data.frame(year = ss3_hake$spr$year, spr = ss3_hake$spr$spr)
ss3 <- ss3[ss3$year %in% 2017:2024, ]
ss3sel <- ss3_hake$sel[ss3_hake$sel$gear %in% gears & ss3_hake$sel$len <= 90, ]
names(ss3sel)[names(ss3sel) == "len"] <- "L"
stk_sex <- stocklen_sex(lfd, lhpar_hake, m_model = "inverse")
```

## Dome-shaped selectivity

The SS3 assessment fits dome-shaped selectivity for all fleets except volpal (longline), which is
logistic. An integrated assessment usually needs such an anchor: at least one fleet with
asymptotic selectivity, because the right-hand side of the domes is confounded with recruitment
and F. FLicc estimates the dome of each fleet from the shape of its own length compositions, so
here the selectivity of every gear, volpal included, is estimated as dome-shaped and compared with
volpal fixed as logistic, as in SS3:

```{r hk-dome}
sf_dome <- c(trawlers = "dsnormal", volpal = "dsnormal", artisanal = "dsnormal", PtSurv = "dsnormal")
sf_logi <- replace(sf_dome, "volpal", "logistic")
fit_sex <- fiticc(lfd, stk_sex, sel_fun = sf_dome, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = c(set, list(linf.sd = 0.1)))
fit_logi <- fiticc(lfd, stk_sex, sel_fun = sf_logi, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                   settings = c(set, list(linf.sd = 0.1)))
rbind(convergence = c(dome = fit_sex$opt$convergence, logistic = fit_logi$opt$convergence),
      neg_loglik = round(c(fit_sex$opt$objective, fit_logi$opt$objective), 1))
```

```{r hk-sel, fig.height = 5}
plot_compare_sel(list("All dome-shaped" = fit_sex, "Volpal logistic (as SS3)" = fit_logi),
                 colours = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00")) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = ss3sel, ggplot2::aes(L, sel), inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = 2)
```

```{r hk-dome-spr, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_spr(list("All dome-shaped" = fit_sex, "Volpal logistic (as SS3)" = fit_logi),
         ci = TRUE, ci_type = "ribbon") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = ss3, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = spr), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.9)
```

The dashed lines are SS3. The length data prefer a dome for volpal as well (lower negative
log-likelihood): large hake are less available to the longlines. With the domes, the shortage of
large females is explained by selectivity rather than by fishing, and SPR is close to the SS3
level in recent years. The wider confidence band of the dome fit is real: it is the uncertainty
about how many large fish there are, which an asymptotic anchor would hide. The all-dome fit is
the base case below.

## Sex-structured versus sex-aggregated

The sex-aggregated fit uses the female life history for all fish, with the survey sexes pooled:

```{r hk-agg}
pool1 <- function(q) { u <- unitSums(q); dimnames(u)$unit <- "unique"; u }
lfd1 <- FLQuants(lapply(lfd, pool1))
lhF <- FLPar(lhpar_hake@.Data[, "F", 1], params = dimnames(lhpar_hake)$params)
fit_agg <- fiticc(lfd1, stocklen(lfd1, lhF, m_model = "inverse"), sel_fun = sf_dome, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = list(obs_model = "mn", surveys = "PtSurv", linf.sd = 0.1))
rbind(convergence = c(sex_structured = fit_sex$opt$convergence, aggregated = fit_agg$opt$convergence),
      female_Linf = round(c(fit_sex$obj$report()$Linf, fit_agg$obj$report()$Linf), 1))
```

```{r hk-spr, fig.height = 4.5}
cmp <- list("Sex-structured" = fit_sex, "Sex-aggregated (female life history)" = fit_agg)
plot_spr(cmp, ci = TRUE, ci_type = "ribbon") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = ss3, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = spr), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.9)
```

Mean SPR by period (SS3 in the first column):

```{r hk-spr-tab}
spr_tab <- function(fits) {
  x <- cbind(SS3 = ss3$spr, sapply(fits, function(f) c(f$report$spr)))
  round(rbind("2017-2020" = colMeans(x[1:4, , drop = FALSE]), "2021-2024" = colMeans(x[5:8, , drop = FALSE])), 3)
}
spr_tab(cmp)
```

Ignoring the sex structure lowers SPR by about 40%. With female growth only, the shortage of fish
above about 75 cm, which in reality is the size only females reach, is read as fishing mortality,
and female Linf is pushed up; the sex-structured model explains part of the shortage by the males,
which stop growing at about 74 cm. 

**Is there evidence in the residuals?** The two models fit the fishery length compositions equally
well:

```{r hk-resid}
fish <- c("trawlers", "volpal", "artisanal")
res_tab <- function(f) {
  r <- resid_flicc(f, type = "osa")
  sapply(fish, function(g) round(sd(r$resid[r$gear == g], na.rm = TRUE), 2))
}
rbind("OSA residual SD, sex-structured" = res_tab(fit_sex), "OSA residual SD, aggregated" = res_tab(fit_agg))
```

```{r hk-resid-len, fig.height = 5}
plot_resid_len(fit_sex, type = "osa", pool_years = TRUE, gear = fish, title = "Sex-structured")
plot_resid_len(fit_agg, type = "osa", pool_years = TRUE, gear = fish, title = "Sex-aggregated")
```

The residuals are almost identical: the aggregated model absorbs the missing males in a larger
Linf, higher F and its selectivity. Residual diagnostics of the commercial length data therefore
cannot reveal that the sex structure is ignored. The evidence comes from the sexed samples (the sex
ratio at length below) and from the life history itself (male growth from otoliths or the
assessment), and the consequence for status is large.

## Fits by sex

```{r hk-len, fig.height = 6}
plot_len(fit_sex, year = 2022:2024)
```

```{r hk-sexratio, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_sexratio(fit_sex)
```

Below 21 cm the survey samples are one composition of both sexes (purple), above it female (red)
and male (blue). The observed proportion of females between 21 and 35 cm is below the
prediction: there are more males at these lengths than the male growth and M of the assessment
imply.

## Penalised estimates of the life history

Linf, M/k and CVL of each sex are fixed unless a penalty is given (chapter *Sex structure*). With
penalties (log-scale SD 0.1) centred on the SS3 values, the length data can move them. The base
case (female Linf penalised) is compared with the SS3 values and with male M/k also estimated:

```{r hk-pen}
fit_fixed <- fiticc(lfd, stk_sex, sel_fun = sf_dome, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = set)
fit_mk <- fiticc(lfd, stk_sex, sel_fun = sf_dome, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                 settings = c(set, list(linf.sd = 0.1, Mk_m.sd = 0.1)))
fits_pen <- list("SS3 values" = fit_fixed, "Female Linf" = fit_sex, "Female Linf and male M/k" = fit_mk)
lh_est <- function(f) {
  r <- f$obj$report()
  c(conv = f$opt$convergence, Linf_F = round(r$Linf, 1), Linf_M = round(r$Linf_m, 1),
    M_M_at_Lref = round(r$Mk_m * c(lhpar_hake["k", "M"]), 3),
    SPR_2024 = round(tail(c(f$report$spr), 1), 3), nll = round(f$opt$objective, 1))
}
t(sapply(fits_pen, lh_est))
```

```{r hk-pen-sexratio, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_sexratio(fit_mk)
```

A lower male M (males surviving better) improves the fit slightly and moves the predicted sex ratio towards
the observations, but not all the way: the remaining excess of males at 21-35 cm points to the male
growth offsets or to a sex ratio at recruitment below 0.5. Female Linf is weakly determined: it
moves down when only female Linf is estimated and up when male M/k is estimated as well, and the
likelihood changes by a few units. Estimating male Linf as well does not converge. The penalties
therefore matter, and the estimates show where the length data point, not values to adopt without
other information (growth studies, tagging). SPR hardly changes.

## What FLicc tells the SS3 assessment

FLicc fits each fleet's length data in seconds, with the same life history as the assessment, so
it is a quick check of structural choices:

* **Volpal selectivity:** the length data prefer a dome to the logistic curve of the assessment;
  FLicc can estimate the domes without an asymptotic anchor, at the price of wider (and honest)
  uncertainty.
* **Sex structure:** ignoring it lowers SPR by about 40%, with no warning in the residuals.
* **Male biology:** the sex ratio at length in PtSurv shows more males at 21-35 cm than the male
  growth and M offsets imply; a lower male M fits better but does not explain all of it.
* **Sexed samples:** small unsexed fish must be combined over sexes (`settings$sex_minlen`, as in
  SS3), or they bias the male parameters.

Each is an SS3 sensitivity run (dome volpal, male M and growth offsets, Linf).

**Limits.** The equilibrium model reads the length structure of each year as the equilibrium at
that year's F. SS3 has the stock rebuilding from very high F, and large females take years to
reappear in the length data, so FLicc cannot follow the trend of SS3 closely (chapter *Fishing
mortality over time*). Length data alone also leave the right-hand side of the domes uncertain.
The CPUE indices of the assessment, which share the selectivity of trawlers and volpal, carry
independent information on the trend; combining them with the length data is the aim of the
planned FLicc-SPM model.
